stories.headline: Trump envoy Witkoff meets Putin in St Petersburg for Ukraine war talks
stories.title: Trump envoy Witkoff meets Putin in St Petersburg for Ukraine war talks
stories.summary: Moscow, Oct 21: US envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday about Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as US President Donald Trump pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting. Witkoff said in televised remarks at the start of the meeting that he hoped to discuss the resumption of the trilateral talks involving the US, Russia and Ukraine that would allow the technical teams to discuss the next steps toward a peace settlement. Putin thanked Trump and Witkoff for their efforts to end the war. The visit came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in the Norwegian capital, Oslo. Witkoff's meetings suggested leaders are keen to bring new momentum to US-led peace efforts, more than 4 ½ years after Russia's army invaded. Efforts by the Trump administration since early last year to end the war have made no significant progress, and there was no suggestion of an imminent breakthrough. Russia and Ukraine are still far apart in their terms for a settlement, as their armies remain locked on the battlefield and they pummel each other with daily long-range strikes. However, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said late Tuesday that the Oslo meeting, which he attended, “made genuine progress.” Witkoff sees some degree of momentum' in peace efforts Witkoff and Putin met at St Petersburg's Constantine Palace, with Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov also at the table. Witkoff said Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner would join the discussion via a video link. Witkoff said he would inform Putin about Tuesday's talks in Oslo, which he described as “productive,” adding that “there is some degree of momentum.” He thanked Putin for lifting Russia's ban on diesel exports, which angered some US lawmakers, adding that it would help reduce prices for US farmers and truckers. Putin said he was ready to discuss prospects for the restoration of US-Russian economic ties, adding that he is also prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran. Moscow is ready to use its special relationship with Tehran to help bring peace, he said. Putin was also due to meet Wednesday with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, who was in St Petersburg meeting with other Russian top officials, the Kremlin said. Russia has cultivated its ties with China, and the two countries last month vetoed a US proposal for UN experts to keep monitoring sanctions on Iran. Norway's prime minister sees a possible new phase' in talks Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations after his trip to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said. “I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy,” Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning. Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he was visiting the country's Parliament and meeting lawmakers. Witkoff appeared to be making another attempt at overcoming hurdles that have kept a deal out of reach. Zelenskyy said Tuesday that on the agenda were future security guarantees for Ukraine, the fate of occupied territories, postwar reconstruction, and the possibility of a ceasefire. Trump said Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in attacks on energy infrastructure but Russia has kept hammering Ukraine's power grid and Kyiv has hit Russian oil refineries. Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war. Trump presses Zelenskyy to compromise Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday that Moscow is willing to listen to new US proposals about Ukraine but he doesn't expect any “miracle” from Washington. At the White House on Tuesday, Trump increased the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again. “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.” If that doesn't happen, “I think it's going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said. Amid fears that Washington was turning its back on Ukraine, Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles, after recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice from allies. The change happened after Zelenskyy spoke with his American counterparts, including a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Russian attacks kill 5 people and injure 25 others, Ukraine says Overnight Russian attacks in Kyiv left three people dead and 12 injured, while 10 residential buildings were damaged, the city's military administration said. Energy facilities were targeted in Kyiv and three other cities in Russian attacks early Wednesday, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Outside the eastern city of Kharkiv, two people died and 11 were wounded when drones exploded in a residential area, he said. The Russian Defence Ministry said that its forces overnight struck a warehouse, an electrical substation and a bulk carrier at sea that was headed to the Ukrainian port of Odesa. The Russian Defence Ministry reported Wednesday that its air defences overnight intercepted 373 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the Black Sea. (AP)

stories.headline: India and the digital quarter-century
stories.title: India and the digital quarter-century
stories.summary: At my first posting in 1977, banking meant handwritten scrolls, ledgers and sheets of carbon paper. I wrote so much that I developed corn on my finger. Today, a street vendor can receive a QR-code payment before the customer has put away the phone. Few contrasts capture India’s transformation more vividly.This is not principally a banking story. It is the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength.From a Large Economy to a Connected OneIn 2000, India’s gross domestic product was about $468 billion. By 2025, it had risen to nearly $3.96 trillion in current-dollar terms, according to the World Bank data. At the end of 2025, India also had more than one billion broadband subscriptions, according to TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India).Connectivity has reduced the cost of distance. A small enterprise can reach customers nationally without first building a national physical network; a migrant worker can transfer money home instantly; and an entrepreneur can begin with cloud software rather than heavy infrastructure. By December 2025, India had more than 2.07 lakh recognised startups, which reported creating over 21.9 lakh direct jobs, according to DPIIT (Department of Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade).The business environment remains a work in progress. Digitising a complicated process does not automatically make it simple. Yet online systems for taxation, company filings, procurement and enterprise registration have widened participation in the formal economy and made markets more accessible.Also Read: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governanceGovernment as a Builder of Digital RailsThe government’s most consequential role has not been to create every digital service. It has been to establish identity, payment and data rails on which public institutions and private businesses can build.Aadhaar, Jan Dhan, mobile connectivity, UPI and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) emerged through coordination among government, regulators, banks, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), technology companies and frontline workers. Policy continuity mattered, as did the preference for interoperable infrastructure rather than isolated, closed systems.The scale is remarkable. As of August 5, the Jan Dhan programme had 58.97 crore beneficiaries; 32.86 crore were women and 45.86 crore were served through rural and semi-urban branches. In FY24–25, UPI processed 185.9 billion transactions worth about ₹260.6 lakh crore. The DBT platform reports cumulative transfers of nearly ₹52.96 lakh crore.These figures illustrate a distinctive Indian model. Government helped build common rails and established trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility. The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation.Reaching the Last MileMy years in banking gave me a front-row seat to this transition, but they also taught me not to confuse a digital launch with a social outcome. An account opened is not necessarily an account used. An application is not inclusive if the customer lacks connectivity, confidence, language support or a reliable way to resolve a problem.In branches and rural communities, I saw that technology worked best when paired with human assistance—business correspondents, self-help groups, trained employees and trusted local institutions. Digital infrastructure should not simply remove people from processes. It should free people from routine work so they can focus on advice, credit, enterprise and problem-solving.That is why grassroots adoption remains central. India’s next phase must invest in digital literacy, accessible design and assisted channels, particularly for women, small farmers, micro-enterprises, older citizens and first-time users.Also Read: Unleashing India's potential over 25 yearsCovid-19: A National Stress TestCovid-19 caused enormous human and economic suffering, but it also revealed the value of India’s digital foundations. Payments, benefit transfers, remote work, online commerce and digital public services became instruments of continuity almost overnight.I had earlier tried to introduce a work-from-home option in banking, especially for employees managing care responsibilities. It encountered resistance because physical presence was often confused with productivity. The pandemic overturned that assumption. When I moved into enterprise technology in 2020, I watched organisations compress years of digital change into months.At the national level, CoWIN provided scheduling, stock tracking and verifiable certificates for a vaccination programme that had administered more than 220 crore doses by January 2023. India also offered the platform as an open-source digital public good to other countries. It showed that software built for Indian scale could have global relevance.From Indian Innovation to a Global ReferenceIndia’s digital public infrastructure is now studied internationally because it offers a model in which the state creates foundational, interoperable systems and public and private providers innovate above them.A G20 report developed with the World Bank observed that India moved transaction-account ownership from roughly one-fourth of adults in 2008 to more than 80 percent—a journey estimated to have taken as long as 47 years without digital public infrastructure.India’s global contribution is, therefore, larger than any single platform. It is the demonstration that population-scale systems can be designed as shared infrastructure. The corresponding responsibility is to ensure that openness and speed are matched by cybersecurity, privacy, consumer protection and accountable governance. Women form the majority in all of Jan Dhan accounts. And SBI holds a major share of all Jan Dhan accounts in India, managing tens of millions of these accounts. Photo by Idrees Mohammed / AFPTurning Access into AgencyThe past 25 years have changed my understanding of technology. I once saw it largely as a means of automating processes. I now see it as an operating system for economic participation.The next wave—powered by artificial intelligence, trusted data and automation—could make Indian businesses more productive and globally competitive. But durable value will require organisations to redesign work, develop skills and retain human judgement. The government must continue to provide enabling infrastructure and clear rules, while enterprise competes, innovates and invests responsibly.India has built an extraordinary infrastructure of access. The test of the next 25 years is whether that access becomes agency: Whether a farmer receives timely credit, a woman entrepreneur reaches a national market, a small business uses AI productively, and every citizen can participate in growth with dignity. That is when digital transformation becomes national transformation.

opening: At my first posting in 1977, banking meant handwritten scrolls, ledgers and sheets of carbon paper.
I wrote so much that I developed corn on my finger.
body: Today, a street vendor can receive a QR-code payment before the customer has put away the phone.
Few contrasts capture India’s transformation more vividly.
This is not principally a banking story.
It is the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength.
From a Large Economy to a Connected.
In 2000, India’s gross domestic product was about $468 billion.
By 2025, it had risen to nearly $3.96 trillion in current-dollar terms, according to the World Bank data.
At the end of 2025, India also had more than one billion broadband subscriptions, according to TRAI (Telecom Regulatory Authority of India).
Connectivity has reduced the cost of distance.

A small enterprise can reach customers nationally without first building a national physical network; a migrant worker can transfer money home instantly; and an entrepreneur can begin with cloud software rather than heavy infrastructure.
By December 2025, India had more than 2.07 lakh recognised startups, which reported creating over 21.9 lakh direct jobs, according to DPIIT (Department of Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade).
The business environment remains a work in progress.
Digitising a complicated process does not automatically make it simple.
Yet online systems for taxation, company filings, procurement and enterprise registration have widened participation in the formal economy and made markets more accessible.
Government as a Builder of Digital Rails.
The government’s most consequential role has not been to create every digital service.
It has been to establish identity, payment and data rails on which public institutions and private businesses can build.

Aadhaar, Jan Dhan, mobile connectivity, UPI and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) emerged through coordination among government, regulators, banks, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), technology companies and frontline workers.
Policy continuity mattered, as did the preference for interoperable infrastructure rather than isolated, closed systems.
The scale is remarkable.
As of August 5, the Jan Dhan programme had 58.97 crore beneficiaries; 32.86 crore were women and 45.86 crore were served through rural and semi-urban branches.
In FY24–25, UPI processed 185.9 billion transactions worth about ₹260.6 lakh crore.
The DBT platform reports cumulative transfers of nearly ₹52.96 lakh crore.
These figures illustrate a distinctive Indian model.
Government helped build common rails and established trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility.
The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation.
Reaching the Last MileMy years in banking gave me a front-row seat to this transition, but they also taught me not to confuse a digital launch with a social outcome.
An account opened is not necessarily an account used.
An application is not inclusive if the customer lacks connectivity, confidence, language support or a reliable way to resolve a problem.
In branches and rural communities, I saw that technology worked best when paired with human assistance—business correspondents, self-help groups, trained employees and trusted local institutions.
Digital infrastructure should not simply remove people from processes.
It should free people from routine work so they can focus on advice, credit, enterprise and problem-solving.
That is why grassroots adoption remains central.
India’s next phase must invest in digital literacy, accessible design and assisted channels, particularly for women, small farmers, micro-enterprises, older citizens and first-time users.
Covid-19: A National Stress TestCovid-19 caused enormous human and economic suffering, but it also revealed the value of India’s digital foundations.
Payments, benefit transfers, remote work, online commerce and digital public services became instruments of continuity almost overnight.
I had earlier tried to introduce a work-from-home option in banking, especially for employees managing care responsibilities.
It encountered resistance because physical presence was often confused with productivity.
The pandemic overturned that assumption.
When I moved into enterprise technology in 2020, I watched organisations compress years of digital change into months.
At the national level, CoWIN provided scheduling, stock tracking and verifiable certificates for a vaccination programme that had administered more than 220 crore doses by January 2023.
India also offered the platform as an open-source digital public good to other countries.
It showed that software built for Indian scale could have global relevance.
From Indian Innovation to a Global Reference.

India’s digital public infrastructure is now studied internationally because it offers a model in which the state creates foundational, interoperable systems and public and private providers innovate above them.

A G20 report developed with the World Bank observed that India moved transaction-account ownership from roughly one-fourth of adults in 2008 to more than 80 percent—a journey estimated to have taken as long as 47 years without digital public infrastructure.
India’s global contribution is, therefore, larger than any single platform.
It is the demonstration that population-scale systems can be designed as shared infrastructure.
The corresponding responsibility is to ensure that openness and speed are matched by cybersecurity, privacy, consumer protection and accountable governance.
Women form the majority in all of Jan Dhan accounts.
And SBI holds a major share of all Jan Dhan accounts in India, managing tens of millions of these accounts.
Photo by Idrees Mohammed / AFPTurning Access into Agency.
The past 25 years have changed my understanding of technology.
I once saw it largely as a means of automating processes.
I now see it as an operating system for economic participation.
The next wave—powered by artificial intelligence, trusted data and automation—could make Indian businesses more productive and globally competitive.
But durable value will require organisations to redesign work, develop skills and retain human judgement.
The government must continue to provide enabling infrastructure and clear rules, while enterprise competes, innovates and invests responsibly.
India has built an extraordinary infrastructure of access.

The test of the next 25 years is whether that access becomes agency: Whether a farmer receives timely credit, a woman entrepreneur reaches a national market, a small business uses AI productively, and every citizen can participate in growth with dignity.
That is when digital transformation becomes national transformation.

A G20 report developed with the World Bank observed that India moved transaction-account ownership from roughly one-fourth of adults in 2008 to more than 80 percent—a journey estimated to have taken as long as 47 years without digital public infrastructure.
And SBI holds a major share of all Jan Dhan accounts in India, managing tens of millions of these accounts.

stories.title: Supreme Court pauses CMRL bribery probe against Pinarayi Vijayan for a week
stories.summary: Supreme Court pauses CMRL bribery probe against Pinarayi Vijayan for a week
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once

article_sentences: The Supreme Court stayed the CMRL bribery investigation against Pinarayi Vijayan and his family for a week.
The pause enables them to challenge the FIR order before a Kerala High Court division bench.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday stayed for a week the investigation against former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan and his family members in the alleged CMRL bribery case, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
CPI(M) state secretary M V Govindan welcomed the decision, saying it upheld the rule of law.
State Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala, however, said the court had not set aside the FIR and claimed that the action taken by the Congress-led UDF government had been proved correct.
In a statement, Chennithala said the investigation had been stayed for a week to allow Vijayan and the others to file an appeal and argue the matter before the Kerala High Court.
Govindan told reporters that the Supreme Court's order was encouraging for the CPI(M), according to PTI.
He said the party had maintained from the beginning that the case was politically motivated and would be challenged both legally and politically.

Govindan claimed that the Supreme Court said the Kerala High Court should have considered the appeal filed by Vijayan, his daughter Veena T and her husband P. A Mohamed Riyas against the October 9 order directing the registration of an FIR against them.
“The rule of law has been upheld by the Supreme Court verdict,” he said.

Chennithala said the state government had carefully examined the Enforcement Directorate's letter seeking the registration of a case against Vijayan, Veena and Riyas under the Prevention of Corruption Act and had not acted in haste.
He said the government had sought legal advice and ordered a preliminary inquiry.

stories.headline: India-US trade deal may be weeks away, but tariff relief and certainty remain key: GTRI’s Srivastava
stories.title: India-US trade deal may be weeks away, but tariff relief and certainty remain key: GTRI’s Srivastava
stories.summary: As India and the US move closer to signing a trade agreement, Ajay Srivastava of GTRI says the key question is whether Washington will offer lower tariffs and protection against future duty hikes.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: An impending India-US trade deal could be finalised soon, with experts noting that tariff cuts, long-term trade certainty, and energy cooperation including Venezuelan crude supplies will be critical to the agreement's success and broader bilateral economic ties.

The proposed India-US trade agreement could be finalised within weeks, but the final outcome will depend on the tariff concessions and long-term trade certainty that Washington offers New Delhi, according to Ajay Srivastava, Founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), and Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, Practice Head for South Asia at Eurasia Group.

Speaking after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the agreement was a matter of weeks, not months, both experts said investors and exporters should closely watch the final terms of the deal rather than the timeline.
They also said energy cooperation, including Venezuelan crude supplies and refinery investments, could become an important pillar of broader India-US economic ties.
"We don't know what the US is going to offer us.
We know what we are going to offer them because we have signed that February joint statement," Srivastava said.
He added that the biggest issue is whether Indian exports will receive lower tariff rates after the agreement.
Srivastava said the current tariff structure remains uncertain across several product categories.
While sectors such as pharmaceuticals and smartphones already enjoy exemptions, labour-intensive exports including garments, textiles and leather continue to face higher duties.
"For example, today our shirts going to the US pay 22% tariff.
After the trade deal, will this be 22% or less?" he said.
He added that exporters would also seek protection against future tariff increases, noting that the US had imposed additional duties on some countries even after signing trade agreements with them.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) held that the YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) had made out a prima facie case in its plea for an extension of time to file nominations for the urban local body elections in Andhra Pradesh.
The party had alleged that its candidates were met with violence and blocked from filing nominations.

The SEC was directed to consider the representations of the party and its candidates, including evidence and material as well as electronic evidence, and to take a decision on extending the last date for filing nominations in urban local bodies wherever it is of the view that candidates were unable to file.

It sought police protection for candidates, an extension of the deadline for filing nominations and the designation of additional and alternative nomination centres to enable candidates to submit their papers safely.

The plea, filed by party general secretary Lella Appireddy through advocate Mahfooz Ahsan Nazki, said several of its candidates were allegedly assaulted and physically prevented from reaching nomination centres during the nomination period, which began on October 16 and ended on October 18.
The High Court had dismissed the party’s application seeking an extension, holding that the deadline had expired and that extending it would amount to interference with the election process.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Quashes Blacklisting Of Drug Supplier Over Quality Failure As Retesting Opportunity Denied
stories.title: Supreme Court Quashes Blacklisting Of Drug Supplier Over Quality Failure As Retesting Opportunity Denied
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has quashed the blacklisting of a pharmaceutical supplier by the Madhya Pradesh government after finding that the authorities failed to follow the mandatory procedure for retesting drug samples before imposing punitive action.

A bench of Justices Vikram Nath, Augustine George Masih and Sandeep Mehta set aside orders blacklisting M/s JPEE Drugs for three years and debarring it from supplying a particular drug for two years after four batches of medicines supplied by the firm were declared Not of Standard Quality (NSQ).

The Court held that the failure to conduct retesting in accordance with the tender conditions, followed by the authorities' failure to comply with the High Court's directions for fresh testing within the stipulated period, deprived the firm of an effective opportunity to challenge the laboratory reports.

"The procedural infirmity, coupled with the irretrievable deprivation of the opportunity for re-testing, renders the orders of blacklisting and debarment unsustainable in law," the Court observed in its October 6 judgment.

The case arose from the supply of Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C) tablets and Ethambutol Hydrochloride tablets to government hospitals and health centres in Madhya Pradesh by JPEE Drugs, a licensed pharmaceutical firm.
In September 2024, the firm received a show-cause notice after three batches of Vitamin C tablets and one batch of Ethambutol Hydrochloride tablets were declared NSQ in laboratory reports.
The firm denied supplying substandard medicines and contended that the quality failures could have resulted from improper storage and handling after delivery.

On September 30, 2024, the Managing Director of the Madhya Pradesh Public Health Services Corporation Limited (MPPHSCL) passed orders directing recovery of the value of the affected batches, blacklisting the firm for three years in respect of the Vitamin C tablets, and debarring it for two years from supplying the Ethambutol Hydrochloride tablets.
The orders stated that no reply had been received from the firm.
A subsequent order dated October 1, 2024, considered and rejected its representation and reiterated the blacklisting and debarment decisions.
Before the Supreme Court, the supplier argued that the authorities had acted without waiting for its reply to the show-cause notice, which had granted seven days to respond.

It also relied on Clause 6 of Annexure IX to the tender document, which required a second sample to be drawn from the same batch and sent to another laboratory if the initial test declared the drug to be of substandard quality.

stories.headline: Q2 FY27: Adani Green Income Rises 39.12% YoY, Profit Up 15.99%
stories.title: Q2 FY27: Adani Green Income Rises 39.12% YoY, Profit Up 15.99%
stories.summary: Adani Green Energy Ltd (AGEL), a pure-play renewable energy (RE) company, has reported a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) decline but a year-on-year (YoY) increase in total income and profit for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. The company reported total income of ₹4,520 crore in Q2 FY27, down 3.07% QoQ from ₹4,663 crore in the June 2026 quarter. However, total income increased 39.12% YoY from ₹3,249 crore in the September 2025 quarter. AGEL's profit for the period stood at ₹747 crore, declining 24.01% QoQ from ₹983 crore in Q1 FY27 but increasing 15.99% YoY from ₹644 crore in Q2 FY26. The company's energy sales increased 32% YoY to 25,747 million units during H1 FY27, supported by the addition of 4,083 MW of renewable energy capacity, a 24% YoY increase in its operational portfolio. Adani Green Expands Battery Storage Capacity AGEL expanded its battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity at Khavda by installing 3,081 MWh during Q2 FY27, taking its total operational storage capacity at the site to 6,632 MWh (6.63 GWh). According to the company, this accounts for more than half of India's operational BESS capacity and makes it the world's largest single-location battery storage installation. With continued additions to its storage portfolio, AGEL may exceed its FY27 guidance of 10 GWh of BESS capacity. Ashish Khanna, CEO of Adani Green Energy, said, “As India’s largest renewable energy company, we take pride in driving the sector’s momentum. This is reflected in our strong execution in H1 FY27, with our operational renewable energy portfolio growing 24% year-on-year to 20.8 GW and energy sales increasing 32%, supporting robust operating performance across our solar, wind and hybrid assets." On the quaterly performance, Khanna said, "Performance during the quarter was equally strong with energy sales increasing 33% year-on-year and revenue from power supply increasing 45% year-on-year to Rs. 4,019 crore while EBITDA from power supply grew 51% YoY." Khanna added, " We also achieved a significant milestone in energy storage, expanding our operational BESS capacity at Khavda to 6.63 GWh—the world’s largest single-location battery storage installation. This makes AGEL India’s largest BESS operator, accounting for more than half of the country’s operational capacity. We remain focused on scaling up storage deployment while closely monitoring the availability of transmission infrastructure.” Adani Green Operational Capacity Grows 24% YoY AGEL's operational renewable energy capacity grew 24% YoY to 20.8 GW, keeping the company on track to achieve its target of 50 GW by 2030. During H1 FY27, AGEL added 4,083 MW of greenfield capacity, comprising 2,957 MW of solar capacity, including 2,568 MW at Khavda in Gujarat and 389 MW in Rajasthan. The company also added 805 MW of wind capacity, comprising 666 MW at Khavda and 139 MW at Mundra, along with 321 MW of solar-wind hybrid capacity at Khavda. The company's energy sales rose 32% YoY to 25,747 million units during H1 FY27, supported by capacity expansion and operating performance across its renewable energy sites. AGEL's operations and maintenance (O&M) activities are supported by its Energy Network Operation Center, which enables real-time monitoring of renewable energy plants across the country. According to the company, this technology has helped maintain high plant availability, increase electricity generation and reduce O&M costs, contributing to an EBITDA margin of 93%. During H1 FY27, AGEL invested approximately ₹17,160 crore in capital expenditure (capex), representing a 38% YoY increase. The company said this reflects its continued focus on capital deployment and long-term growth. Adani Green's Khavda Capacity Reaches 10.8 GW AGEL's operational capacity at Khavda has increased to 10.8 GW from 7.1 GW a year earlier. The company said its investments in BESS are also helping address curtailment challenges at the site by providing greater flexibility in managing renewable energy generation. The operational portfolio at Khavda now stands at 10,752 MW across solar, wind and hybrid projects. With continued workforce deployment, a localised supply chain and technologies such as robotic solar module installation, AGEL aims to achieve 30 GW of renewable energy capacity at Khavda by 2029. The company expects its execution capabilities and use of advanced technologies to support the development of renewable energy capacity at this scale.

article_sentences: The Tamil Nadu government, on Wednesday (October 21, 2026), issued an order sanctioning ₹71.01 crore to enhance the contingency funds provided to all police stations in the State to meet routine administrative and operational expenses.

According to an official press release, Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay had announced the enhancement of contingency funds to all police stations during the demand for grants for the Home Department for 2026-27 in the Legislative Assembly.
Accordingly, the State government has issued an order allocating the amount with the objective meet unforeseen expenses and eliminate corruption, the release said.
Police stations are classified into three categories based on the number of crimes reported.

The monthly contingency fund for Light category police stations has been increased from ₹3,750 to ₹30,000, for Medium police stations from ₹6,000 to ₹40,000, and for heavy police stations from ₹8,250 to ₹50,000, the release added.

stories.headline: Delhi HC refuses relief to CJP leaders challenging judicial custody
stories.title: Delhi HC refuses relief to CJP leaders challenging judicial custody
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 21: The Delhi High Court on Wednesday refused to interfere with the judicial custody of Cockroach Janta Party leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, as it asked them to await the outcome of the hearing scheduled before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM), and approach the appellate court if their grievance continues. The hearing before the SEM is scheduled later in the day. Justice Subramonium Prasad permitted the CJP co-conveners to withdraw their plea and observed that a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution was not an appropriate remedy for a "repeat case" of violating a 'peace' bond. Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Chetan Sharma said the matter is listed before the SEM regarding the furnishing of fresh sureties. The case was taken up by the court after the CJP leaders sought an urgent hearing in the high court, which is shut due to the Dussehra break. Along with other CJP workers, Das and Ranka displayed the national flag at Jantar Mantar, which had been denotified as a protest site, and shouted slogans against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar before being detained and placed under preventive arrest on October 13. A SEM first sent them to judicial custody for five days on October 14. Advocate Abhik Chimni, appearing for the petitioners, argued that they ought to be released on a personal bond as the SEM has no jurisdiction to extend their judicial custody. He further argued that the SEM's insistence on a surety was not sustained in law. Justice Prasad, however, observed that the petitioners allegedly violated a bond tendered by them for maintaining tranquillity by entering a de-notified protest site, and questioned whether the authorities were not entitled to seek a "stricter" surety in a "repeat case". The judge remarked that the questions surrounding the locus and motive of the petitioners were also significant and have to be looked into by the appropriate authority, considering that while they were initially involved in a student protest, there was now a different cause and a statement about "regime change". "Now there is another cause. People remain the same, causes change. All these questions assume significance so to who you are; what is your motive; what are you trying to do? You suddenly hear something like a regime change.. you suddenly hear something (against) which we normally do by a ballot. In a hearing like this, it is not necessary for us to go into this. Keep the debate for an appropriate proceeding," the judge said. On being informed that Das and Ranka were 27 and 31 years old, respectively, the court remarked, "That means you are not Gen-Z." "They are an inspiration," the lawyer responded. The court also emphasised that the purpose behind a police permission for a protest is not to stop anyone but prevent "unwanted persons" from joining the protest group and ensure that a peaceful agitation does not escalate into violence. "The two petitioners here are at the forefront. When you go and break a barricade, the chances of 10 or 20 more people violating the 163 (prohibitory order) are very bright. There might be persons who might not be in your control and who might do things. We have seen it happening outside our country. Student protest has now gone into arson, looting, burning," it added. While permitting Das and Ranka to withdraw the case, the judge clarified that he has not made observations on the merit of the matter. Das and Ranka assailed the SEM's October 19 order remanding them to two days' judicial custody in the high court. They were taken into custody on October 13 after they allegedly climbed over a locked gate to enter Jantar Mantar, which had earlier been denotified as a designated protest site, and were sent to five-day judicial custody. A newly-appointed Special Executive Magistrate at Mandir Marg police station on Monday ordered their judicial remand till October 21 after they were produced before him. In their petition, the CJP leaders argued that the SEM's order is illegal, arbitrary and liable to be set aside. Their petition asserted that Das and Ranka continue to remain in custody for six days despite submitting the required sureties multiple times. "The mandatory procedure under Section 140 BNSS was not followed for rejecting the surety showing complete misapplication of the law in the impugned order. That delay and obstruction in the acceptance and verification of sureties frustrates the very purpose of release," the plea said. "The learned SEM has arbitrarily exercised their powers to extend judicial custody of the petitioners under Section 135(3) BNSS. This is because the basis of judicial custody is 'in default of execution of the bond'. However, the basis is incorrect in view of the petitioner's sureties produced on 19.10.2026 being in accordance with law," it added.

That delay and obstruction in the acceptance and verification of sureties frustrates the very purpose of release," the plea said.
"The learned SEM has arbitrarily exercised their powers to extend judicial custody of the petitioners under Section 135(3) BNSS.
This is because the basis of judicial custody is 'in default of execution of the bond'.
However, the basis is incorrect in view of the petitioner's sureties produced on 19.10.2026 being in accordance with law," it added.

sentences.text: Along with other CJP workers, Das and Ranka displayed the national flag at Jantar Mantar, which had been denotified as a protest site, and shouted slogans against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar before being detained and placed under preventive arrest on October 13.
A newly-appointed Special Executive Magistrate at Mandir Marg police station on Monday ordered their judicial remand till October 21 after they were produced before him.

New Delhi, Oct 21: The Delhi High Court on Wednesday refused to interfere with the judicial custody of Cockroach Janta Party leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, as it asked them to await the outcome of the hearing scheduled before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM), and approach the appellate court if their grievance continues.
A SEM first sent them to judicial custody for five days on October 14.
